domain_restrictions: S is closed under addition: ∀a,b ∈ S, a+b ∈ S
N0 \ S is finite (numerical semigroup property)
m is defined as least positive element of S: m = min(S ∩ N+)
m ≥ 1 (note: if m=1 then the condition 1 ≤ r ≤ m-1 yields an empty range)
r is an integer with 1 ≤ r ≤ m-1
Leastness for w_r is with respect to the usual order on N0 (i.e., among elements of S congruent to r mod m, w_r has minimal value)
Ap(S,m) = { s ∈ S : s - m ∉ S } (with s - m interpreted in integers; equivalently require that s ≥ m or, if s < m, then automatically s-m ∉ S because S ⊆ N0)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any numerical semigroup S ⊆ N0 and m = min(S ∩ N+) (with m ≥ 1), for every integer r with 1 ≤ r ≤ m-1 there exists a unique element w_r ∈ S such that w_r ≡ r (mod m) and w_r is the least element of S in that congruence class. With Ap(S,m) defined by Ap(S,m) = { s ∈ S : s−m ∉ S }, the Apéry set satisfies Ap(S,m) = {0} ∪ {w_r : 1 ≤ r ≤ m-1}. Moreover, for each such r, there exists a unique positive integer k_r such that w_r = r + m k_r (and positivity holds because r < m and m is the least positive element of S, so r ∉ S and thus w_r > r).
quantifier_order: ∀ S (numerical-semigroup conditions) ... let m = min(S ∩ N+) ... ∀ r (1 ≤ r ≤ m-1) ∃! w_r ∈ S such that (w_r ≡ r (mod m) ∧ w_r is least in its congruence class w.r.t. ≤)
Then (by definition of Ap(S,m)) set equality: Ap(S,m) = {0, w_1, ..., w_{m-1}}
For each r (1 ≤ r ≤ m-1): ∃! k_r ∈ N+ such that w_r = r + m k_r

payload.statement_nl: Let S be a subset of N0 = {0,1,2,...} such that 0 belongs to S, S is closed under addition, and N0 \ S is finite; in other words, S is a numerical semigroup. Let m be the least positive element of S, and assume m >= 1. Then for every integer r with 1 <= r <= m-1, there exists a unique least element w_r of S that is congruent to r modulo m. If the Apéry set with respect to m is defined by Ap(S,m) = {s in S : s - m is not in S}, then Ap(S,m) = {0, w_1, ..., w_{m-1}}. Moreover each w_r can be written uniquely in the form w_r = r + m k_r for a positive integer k_r.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Let S be a numerical semigroup, so S \subseteq \mathbb N_0, 0\in S, S is closed under addition, and \mathbb N_0\setminus S is finite. Let m be the least positive element of S. We must prove three things:

(1) for each integer r with 1\le r\le m-1, there exists a unique least element w_r\in S congruent to r mod m;
(2) Ap(S,m)={0,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}};
(3) each w_r has a unique representation w_r=r+mk_r with k_r\in \mathbb N_+.

First, fix r with 1\le r\le m-1.

Existence of some element of S congruent to r modulo m: since \mathbb N_0\setminus S is finite, there exists an integer N such that every n\ge N belongs to S. Choose t large enough that r+tm\ge N. Then r+tm\in S, and clearly r+tm\equiv r\pmod m. Thus the set
A_r:=\{s\in S: s\equiv r\pmod m\}
is nonempty.

Since A_r is a nonempty subset of \mathbb N_0, by well-ordering it has a least element. Call it w_r. This proves existence of a least element in the congruence class r modulo m.

Uniqueness of w_r is immediate: a subset of \mathbb N_0 has at most one least element. Hence for each r with 1\le r\le m-1 there exists a unique least element w_r\in S such that w_r\equiv r\pmod m.

Now we prove the description of the Ap\'ery set.
Recall
Ap(S,m)=\{s\in S: s-m\notin S\}.

We first show that 0\in Ap(S,m). Indeed, 0\in S, and 0-m=-m\notin S because S\subseteq \mathbb N_0. Hence 0\in Ap(S,m).

Next, for each r with 1\le r\le m-1, we show w_r\in Ap(S,m). Since w_r\equiv r\pmod m, we have w_r\ne 0, so w_r\ge 1. If w_r-m\in S, then because w_r\equiv r\pmod m, also w_r-m\equiv r\pmod m; and since m is positive, w_r-m<w_r. This contradicts the minimality of w_r in A_r. Therefore w_r-m\notin S, so w_r\in Ap(S,m).

Thus {0,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}}\subseteq Ap(S,m).

For the reverse inclusion, let s\in Ap(S,m). We show s is one of these elements. Consider the residue class of s modulo m.

If s\equiv 0\pmod m, then s=qm for some q\in \mathbb N_0. Because s\in S and m\in S, if q\ge 1 then s-m=(q-1)m\in S (for q=1 this is 0\in S; for q>1 it is a sum of q-1 copies of m, hence in S by closure). But this contradicts s\in Ap(S,m). Therefore q=0, so s=0.

If instead s\equiv r\pmod m for some r with 1\le r\le m-1, then s\in A_r. Since w_r is the least element of A_r, we have w_r\le s. Also s-w_r is divisible by m, so s=w_r+tm for some integer t\ge 0. If t\ge 1, then s-m=w_r+(t-1)m. Because w_r\in S and m\in S, closure of S under addition gives s-m\in S, contradicting s\in Ap(S,m). Hence t=0, so s=w_r.

Therefore every element s\in Ap(S,m) is either 0 or one of the w_r. Hence
Ap(S,m)=\{0,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}\}.

Finally, fix r with 1\le r\le m-1. Since w_r\equiv r\pmod m, there exists an integer k_r such that
w_r=r+mk_r.
This k_r is unique because if r+mk=r+mk', then m(k-k')=0, hence k=k'. It remains to show k_r is a positive integer.

Because 1\le r\le m-1 and m is the least positive element of S, we must have r\notin S. Indeed, if r were in S, then r would be a positive element of S smaller than m, impossible. But w_r\in S and w_r\equiv r\pmod m. If w_r=r, then r\in S, impossible. So w_r>r. Since w_r-r is a multiple of m, we have w_r-r=mk_r with k_r\in \mathbb Z and w_r-r>0; therefore k_r>0. Hence k_r\in \mathbb N_+.

So for each r with 1\le r\le m-1, there exists a unique positive integer k_r such that w_r=r+mk_r.

All claimed statements are proved.
result_payload.proof_summary: Using cofiniteness of a numerical semigroup, each nonzero residue class modulo m contains some element of S; well-ordering gives a unique least such element w_r. Minimality shows w_r-m\notin S, so w_r lies in the Ap\'ery set. Conversely, any s in Ap(S,m) cannot be a positive multiple of m, hence if s\equiv0 mod m then s=0; if s\equiv r mod m with 1\le r\le m-1, then writing s=w_r+tm forces t=0, otherwise s-m\in S. Thus Ap(S,m)={0,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}}. Finally, congruence gives w_r=r+mk_r for a unique integer k_r, and since r<m is not in S while w_r\in S, one has w_r>r, so k_r>0.

used_external_facts: Well-ordering principle for nonempty subsets of \mathbb N_0.
If a set has finite complement in \mathbb N_0, then all sufficiently large nonnegative integers belong to the set.
